items.q: What is the core premise of Zero Trust?
choices: Never trust, always verify — no implicit trust by location
Trust is established once per session
items.explain: Zero Trust removes implicit trust: every access decision is verified regardless of network location (NIST SP 800-207).

items.q: In NIST SP 800-207, which component decides whether to grant access?
choices: Policy Engine (within the Policy Decision Point)
items.explain: The Policy Decision Point (policy engine + policy administrator) decides; the Policy Enforcement Point enables/denies the connection.

items.q: Application allowlisting is best described as:
choices: Permitting only approved applications and denying everything else by default
items.explain: Allowlisting inverts the model: default-deny with explicit approval, so unknown malware and ransomware executables are blocked.

choices: What the application can interact with — files, registry, network, other apps
items.explain: Ringfencing places a boundary around an app's interactions, stopping attackers from weaponizing legitimate tools like PowerShell.

items.q: Which technique steals service-account hashes from Kerberos TGS responses?
items.explain: Kerberoasting requests service tickets and cracks them offline; the fix is strong, managed service-account passwords.

items.q: The tiered administration model exists to:
choices: Prevent credential theft from spreading by separating privilege tiers
items.explain: Tiering (0/1/2) ensures a compromise at one tier cannot harvest credentials valid at a higher tier.

items.q: Before enforcing allowlisting in production, ThreatLocker-style deployments run:
choices: Learning mode to baseline normal application behavior
items.explain: Learning mode observes normal operations for ~a week so policies reflect reality before deny-by-default enforcement.

items.q: Which CISA ZTMM pillar covers privileged access management?
items.explain: Identity is the pillar covering authentication, privileged access, and continuous validation of users and service accounts.

items.q: A SHA-256 hash is primarily used to verify:
choices: Data integrity — the file has not changed
items.explain: Hashes detect tampering: any change to the input produces a different digest (file-integrity monitoring).

items.q: In the OWASP Top 10, SQL injection falls under:
items.explain: Injection covers untrusted input interpreted as commands — SQLi, command injection, and similar flaws.

items.q: The strongest defense against credential phishing is:
choices: Phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO2) plus technical email controls
items.explain: Training helps, but phishing-resistant MFA and technical controls catch what humans miss — defense in depth.

items.q: Storage Control that limits share access by application defeats ransomware by:
choices: Blocking untrusted apps from reaching files they have no business touching
items.explain: Ransomware must run as some process; if that process isn't approved for the share, encryption is denied at the boundary.
